MSK–SKIN · MODULE II · PATHOLOGY

Soft Tissue Tumors

Lecture Companion · Classification → morphology → molecular signatures → clinical behavior

ObjectivesApproachLipogenicFibrogenicSmooth muscleSkeletal muscleUncertainFinal mastery

Learning objectives

  1. Review the basic WHO 2020 lineage-based classification of soft-tissue tumors.
  2. Differentiate lipoma from liposarcoma.
  3. Describe superficial and deep fibromatosis, including behavior and pathogenesis.
  4. Differentiate leiomyoma from leiomyosarcoma.
  5. Recognize rhabdomyoma and distinguish embryonal from alveolar rhabdomyosarcoma.
  6. Recognize synovial sarcoma and the lecture’s category of undifferentiated soft-tissue sarcoma.

Big picture

Soft-tissue tumors are mesenchymal proliferations grouped by the tissue they resemble, not simply by where they occur. Lineage explains the vocabulary; biologic behavior explains the clinical stakes. A fatty tumor can be a benign lipoma or malignant liposarcoma, while fibromatosis can invade and recur without metastasizing. Diagnose with the combination of location, age, morphology, and when available a characteristic molecular alteration.

MUST KNOW
A mass that grows slowly and does not hurt can still be malignant. Evaluate size, depth, growth and imaging; do not use pain as a reassuring discriminator.

Objective 1 · Classify, recognize and safely approach a soft-tissue mass

WHO 2020 framework taught in this lecture: adipose, fibrous, smooth muscle, skeletal muscle, and uncertain differentiation. Benign tumors greatly outnumber malignant tumors. The sarcomas are rare (the lecture estimates roughly 12,000 US cases annually).

LineageBenignIntermediate / locally aggressiveMalignant
AdiposeLipoma—Liposarcoma
FibrousNodular fasciitisFibromatosisFibrosarcoma
Smooth muscleLeiomyoma—Leiomyosarcoma
Skeletal muscleRhabdomyoma—Rhabdomyosarcoma
Uncertain differentiation——Synovial sarcoma; undifferentiated soft-tissue sarcoma

Presentation and prognosis

Lecture figures: 85% adult / 15% pediatric soft-tissue sarcomas; locations 60% extremities (lower more than upper), 20% trunk, 15% retroperitoneum, 5% head/neck. Typically a slow-growing, painless mass. Pediatric: rhabdomyosarcoma; adult: liposarcoma; young adult: synovial sarcoma; older adult: undifferentiated sarcoma.

Concerning presentation: greater than a golf ball in a proximal extremity or a marble in the hand/foot warrants imaging (lecture rule). Larger, deeper, higher-grade, or metastatic lesions predict worse outcomes. Metastasis is primarily hematogenous to lung; lymphatic metastasis is uncommon (~5%, with certain exceptions including alveolar rhabdomyosarcoma). MRI findings may be nonspecific.

Pathology, grade, stage, and margins

Malignant patterns tend toward large/deep/infiltrative growth, increased cellularity, atypia, frequent or atypical mitoses, and necrosis/hemorrhage. FNCLCC grading uses differentiation, mitotic count, and necrosis; the lecture flags rhabdomyosarcoma as grade 3 by default. Histologic typing/grade help estimate distant spread and survival; resection margins predict local recurrence; staging guides management. The specific site-based T categories on slide 8 are marked for familiarity only.

Biopsy and treatment principles

The lecturer specifically warns against poorly planned biopsy: use a short longitudinal incision, a route through muscle where appropriate, meticulous hemostasis, and any drain in line with the incision. Biopsy should be planned by the surgeon/team capable of definitive resection so the biopsy tract can be handled appropriately. Surgery is the mainstay, typically wide limb-sparing excision when feasible; radiation is commonly used, and chemotherapy has an especially important role in rhabdomyosarcoma. Treatment varies by histology and risk.

CLINICAL CONNECTION
A poorly placed biopsy tract may contaminate additional tissue compartments and complicate limb-sparing surgery. Referral to a sarcoma team before biopsy is the practical implication.
RETRIEVAL CHECKPOINT · What predicts lung metastases, and what predicts local recurrence?

Histologic type and grade help predict distant metastasis and overall survival; surgical margin status helps predict local recurrence.

RETRIEVAL CHECKPOINT · Why can an apparently painless mass still need imaging?

Sarcomas often grow slowly and painlessly; depth, size and growth pattern are more informative than pain alone.

Objective 2 · Lipogenic tumors: lipoma versus liposarcoma

Lipoma — benign fat

The most common soft-tissue tumor in adults. Usually age 40–60, subcutaneous proximal extremities or trunk, mobile, slowly enlarging and painless, generally solitary. It is circumscribed, soft, yellow/greasy, composed of mature benign adipocytes. Simple excision is curative; recurrence is rare except occasional intramuscular lipomas. The lecture specifically contrasts this with a retroperitoneal fat mass, which should not casually be called a lipoma.

Liposarcoma — malignant adipocytic tumor

The lecture calls this the most common soft-tissue sarcoma in adults, typically fifth to sixth decade. A large (>5–10 cm), deep proximal thigh or retroperitoneal mass may look fatty grossly but contains firmer fibrous regions; necrosis may appear in high-grade disease.

FeatureWell-differentiated / ALT (50%)Myxoid (20%)
Lecture grade12
Common siteALT: deep proximal extremity; WDLPS: retroperitoneumDeep proximal extremity / thigh
HistologyAdipocytic proliferation with atypical stromal cellsLipoblasts, myxoid stroma, branching “chicken-wire” capillaries
MolecularMDM2 (12q) and/or CDK4 amplificationt(12;16), FUS–DDIT3 fusion
ProgressionDedifferentiated fibroblastic componentRound-cell component
Clinical behavior per lectureALT extremity: local recurrence; retroperitoneal WDLPS: recurrence and adverse outcomeRecurrence/metastasis; worse with round-cell morphology
EXAM TRAP
ALT versus WDLPS: the lecture uses site-specific nomenclature for the same well-differentiated family. Deep extremity lesions and retroperitoneal lesions behave differently because complete excision is more difficult in the retroperitoneum.
BOARD / CLINICAL ENRICHMENT
Atypical adipocytes/lipoblasts alone are not sufficient for every diagnosis; integration of specimen morphology, site, and molecular testing improves reliability. This is explanatory context beyond the slide.
RETRIEVAL CHECKPOINT · What molecular findings distinguish the two featured liposarcomas?

Well-differentiated: MDM2/CDK4 amplification. Myxoid: FUS–DDIT3 fusion, t(12;16).

Objective 3 · Fibromatosis: non-metastasizing but infiltrative

Key mental model: bland fibroblasts and collagen can locally invade surrounding structures without acquiring the metastatic behavior of a sarcoma. Therefore “benign histology” does not imply “easy to remove.”

Superficial fibromatosis

FormLocation / patientHallmark
Palmar (Dupuytren)Adults; often bilateralPalmar fibrosis → finger flexion contractures
Plantar (Ledderhose)Lecture emphasizes pediatric, often unilateralPlantar fibrous nodule
Penile (Peyronie)Adult dorsal penisPlaque/mass → abnormal curvature, occasionally obstruction

Recurrence after excision is common. The lecture notes association with Northern European descent.

Deep fibromatosis / desmoid tumor

Often abdominal wall or mesentery in teens/young adults, with an association noted in postpartum women. Grossly firm and gray-white, infiltrating muscle and fat. Histology: bland spindle-shaped fibroblasts in collagen-containing fascicles, extending peripherally into adjacent tissue. Frequent local recurrence and difficulty with excision, but no metastases. The lecture lists COX-2 inhibitors and tamoxifen as medical approaches.

Pathogenesis: CTNNB1 / β-catenin signaling is implicated; the lecture associates inherited disease with Gardner syndrome.

FIRST AID CONNECTION
Desmoid tumors can be associated with familial adenomatous polyposis/Gardner syndrome; think of the APC–β-catenin pathway when the lesion occurs with an inherited polyposis syndrome. Distinguish sporadic CTNNB1 alterations from germline APC-associated disease.
COMMON CONFUSION
Desmoid ≠ fibrosarcoma. Desmoid is locally aggressive and recurrent but nonmetastasizing; a malignant sarcoma has potential to metastasize.
RETRIEVAL CHECKPOINT · Why is desmoid clinically problematic even though the fibroblasts look bland?

Its infiltrative growth enters muscle and fat, making complete removal difficult and recurrence frequent; it does not metastasize.

Objective 4 · Smooth-muscle tumors

Leiomyoma

Benign smooth-muscle tumor, most often uterine (“fibroid”), but also skin, GI tract and deep soft tissues. May be asymptomatic or cause pain; uterine lesions can cause irregular menstrual bleeding and infertility. Grossly well circumscribed with whorled cut surface. Microscopically intersecting/whorled fascicles of bland spindle cells with blunt-ended cigar-shaped nuclei.

Leiomyosarcoma

Malignant smooth-muscle tumor (lecture: 10–20% of soft-tissue sarcomas) in adults around age 50–70, particularly postmenopausal women. Sites include uterus, retroperitoneum and extremities. The lecture emphasizes that it arises de novo, not through malignant transformation of a leiomyoma. It retains smooth-muscle architecture but adds pleomorphism, increased mitotic activity and necrosis. Most are high grade; retroperitoneal site confers a worse prognosis.

DON’T MIX THESE UP
Both tumors can show whorled fascicles and cigar-shaped nuclei. Distinguish malignancy by mitoses, atypia and tumor-cell necrosis, not by spindle shape alone.
RETRIEVAL CHECKPOINT · Does a uterine leiomyosarcoma usually arise from a pre-existing leiomyoma?

No. The lecture specifically describes leiomyosarcoma as arising de novo.

Objective 5 · Skeletal-muscle tumors and rhabdomyosarcoma

Rhabdomyoma

Rare benign skeletal-muscle-lineage tumor. The lecture identifies cardiac rhabdomyoma in children with tuberous sclerosis (firm, pale nodules) and extracardiac head-and-neck/oral cavity rhabdomyoma more often in adults.

Rhabdomyosarcoma (RMS)

Most common pediatric soft-tissue sarcoma. Histologic grade 3 in both lecture-featured subtypes. Sarcoma cells exhibit skeletal muscle differentiation, but this does not mean the mass must originate within a mature skeletal muscle.

FeatureEmbryonal RMS (60%)Alveolar RMS (20%)
Typical patientChild <15 yearsYoung adult
SiteHead and neck / genitourinaryDeep extremity (thigh)
GrossBotryoid (“grape-like”) variantExpansile mass
HistologyRhabdomyoblasts: strap/tadpole/spider; cambium layer in botryoid variantAlveolar-like architecture, rounded cells with scant cytoplasm
MolecularLecture: nonspecific copy number changes; no characteristic fusiont(2;13), PAX3–FOXO fusion (as abbreviated in course slide)
PrognosisBetter with multimodal therapyPoorer
FIRST AID CONNECTION
Rhabdomyosarcoma is a classic pediatric sarcoma; rhabdomyoblasts express skeletal muscle markers such as desmin. Alveolar RMS is linked to PAX–FOXO1 family fusions; Step 1 questions often contrast this with embryonal/botryoid tumors.
LECTURE → STEP 1 BRIDGE
Child + genitourinary grape-like mass → embryonal rhabdomyosarcoma (sarcoma botryoides) → strap/tadpole rhabdomyoblasts and cambium layer. Deep thigh mass + alveolar histology + PAX fusion → alveolar subtype.
RETRIEVAL CHECKPOINT · A child has a grape-like mass near the bladder. Which subtype and microscopic features?

Embryonal RMS, botryoid variant; cambium layer and rhabdomyoblasts with strap/tadpole morphology.

RETRIEVAL CHECKPOINT · What separates alveolar from embryonal RMS molecularly in the lecture?

Alveolar: t(2;13) PAX3–FOXO fusion (course wording). Embryonal: no defining fusion in the course comparison.

Objective 6 · Tumors of uncertain differentiation

Synovial sarcoma

Misnomer: not derived from synovium, despite frequently being near joints. The lecture reports about 10% of soft-tissue sarcomas, often ages 20–50 and deep extremities—particularly near the knee (60–70%)—but also chest wall and head/neck. Histology may be biphasic (spindle-cell and gland-forming epithelial components) or monophasic. Molecular hallmark: t(X;18), SS18–SSX fusion. Aggressive behavior and metastases to lung and bone. The lecture lists surgery and chemotherapy.

EXAM TRAP
A periarticular sarcoma is not necessarily a tumor of synovial origin. Prioritize SS18–SSX and biphasic or monophasic histology over the name.

Undifferentiated soft-tissue sarcoma (USTS)

The lecture lists USTS in the WHO classification and identifies undifferentiated sarcoma among age-stratified sarcomas of older adults, but does not provide a dedicated histologic or molecular profile. Do not invent a lecture-specific immunostain or gene signature here. Conceptually, “undifferentiated” indicates that a distinct lineage has not been established.

RETRIEVAL CHECKPOINT · A young adult has a deep mass near the knee with t(X;18). Why is “synovial” potentially misleading?

Synovial sarcoma is a tumor of uncertain differentiation and does not originate from synovium; SS18–SSX is the lecture’s hallmark.

MSK CONNECTION
A deep thigh or peri-knee mass should connect the pathology differential to the anatomic compartment, MRI interpretation and biopsy planning. This lecture treats the imaging as often nonspecific; pathology and molecular findings settle the subtype.

Master these before moving on

  1. Lineage ≠ behavior. A tumor can resemble fat, muscle or fibroblasts; separately decide whether it is benign, locally aggressive or metastatic. Essential for all differentials.
  2. Location and depth matter. The same fatty appearance has different implications in superficial subcutaneous tissue versus a deep thigh or retroperitoneum. Essential for triage.
  3. Blunt-ended spindle nuclei are not enough. Leiomyoma and leiomyosarcoma share smooth-muscle architecture; necrosis and mitoses change the diagnosis.
  4. Fibromatosis is an intermediate category. Local invasion and recurrence can occur without metastasis. Essential to interpret “benign but infiltrative.”
  5. Remember the subtype signature. MDM2/CDK4, FUS–DDIT3, β-catenin, PAX3–FOXO and SS18–SSX connect histology to clinicopathology.

The most useful First Aid connections

  1. Desmoid tumor ↔ APC/FAP/Gardner pathway and β-catenin signaling.
  2. Cardiac rhabdomyoma ↔ pediatric tuberous sclerosis.
  3. Embryonal botryoid RMS ↔ pediatric genitourinary grape-like lesion.
  4. Alveolar RMS ↔ PAX–FOXO1 fusion biology.
  5. Synovial sarcoma ↔ SS18–SSX fusion, despite misleading name.
